result: FlpStop is a generalizable tool for conditional gene disruption and rescue in post-mitotic cells. The authors tested FlpStop in eight genes (ap, cac, ChAT, Gad1, para, Rdl, Shal, VGlut), generating five conditional null alleles and two conditional hypomorphs. FlpStop can efficiently impair gene function within genetically targeted populations and at specific times during development, with positive labeling of targeted cells through tdTomato expression.
evaluation: Claims C2, C41-C47 are strongly supported by extensive experimental validation across multiple genes (Figures 2-7, Table 1). The approach successfully produced conditional null alleles for 5/8 genes tested (cac, Gad1, para, Rdl, ap) and hypomorphs for 2/8 genes (VGlut, Shal), with only ChAT showing no disruption. Complementation tests, qRT-PCR, paralysis assays, and temporal control experiments (Figure 2) collectively demonstrate both spatial and temporal control of gene function. The tdTomato reporter successfully labels manipulated cells (Figures 4-6).

result: Conditional null alleles of Gad1, Rdl, cac, and para were successfully produced using FlpStop. For Gad1 and Rdl, the disrupting alleles were lethal when combined with independent null alleles, demonstrating complete gene disruption. For cac and para (X-chromosome genes), disrupting alleles were hemizygous/homozygous lethal and showed severe paralysis phenotypes with temperature-sensitive alleles.
evaluation: Claims C3-C6, C107-C108, C136 are well-supported by complementation tests (Figure 3a,b), paralysis assays (Figure 3c,d), and qRT-PCR showing ~50% transcript reduction in heterozygotes (Figure 3f-i). The lethality data for Gad1 and Rdl with two independent null alleles each provides strong evidence for complete disruption. Temperature-sensitive complementation tests for para and cac show more severe phenotypes than homozygous temperature-sensitive mutants, supporting null or near-null status.

result: FlpStop targeting of apterous produced two alleles (non-disrupting and disrupting). The non-disrupting allele (apFlpStop ND) combined with a null allele produced 99% wild-type wings (n=462), demonstrating no interference with gene function. The disrupting allele (apFlpStop D) combined with the null allele produced 97% wingless flies (n=236), as severe as homozygous null flies, demonstrating complete gene disruption. Neither allele showed dominant negative effects when combined with wild-type chromosomes.
evaluation: Claims C66-C73 are strongly supported by complementation test data (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The quantitative wing phenotype scoring provides clear evidence that the non-disrupting allele is functionally wild-type and the disrupting allele is a complete null. The comparison to homozygous null flies and heterozygous combinations with wild-type chromosomes provides appropriate controls. Sample sizes are adequate (n=236-462 wings).

result: FlpStop enables temporal control of gene disruption and rescue. Heat-shock induction of Flp at different developmental time points (days 1-7) in apFlpStop ND/apUG035 flies showed that early disruption (days 1-3) caused severe wing phenotypes including complete wing loss, while later disruption produced less severe phenotypes. Conversely, early rescue (day 1) of apFlpStop D/apUG035 flies restored wild-type wings in >50% of cases, but later rescue (days 4-7) could not rescue the wingless phenotype. The time window for necessity differs from the time window for sufficiency of apterous function.
evaluation: Claims C76-C83 are supported by temporal control experiments (Figure 2c-e) with appropriate sample sizes across multiple time points. The differential effects of disruption versus rescue timing are clearly demonstrated and consistent with established developmental biology of apterous (C77, C84-C85 cite Cohen et al., 1992; Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993). The observation that necessity and sufficiency windows differ (C83) is a valid inference from the data comparing Figure 2d and 2e.

result: Tissue-specific inversion of the FlpStop cassette in apterous strongly impaired Apterous protein expression in wing imaginal discs. TdTomato-positive regions lacked Apterous immunostaining while other regions of the same disc showed high protein expression levels.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d) showing clear spatial correlation between tdTomato expression and loss of Apterous protein. The comparison to wild-type discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b) and non-heat-shocked controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c) provides appropriate controls. This demonstrates protein-level disruption in addition to the phenotypic and mRNA-level evidence.

result: All non-disrupting FlpStop alleles (ChAT, Gad1, Rdl, VGlut, cac, para) were viable when combined with null alleles and produced adult flies at expected rates, demonstrating no phenotypic effect in the non-disrupting orientation. No evidence of dominant negative activity was observed as measured by heterozygous lethality.
evaluation: Claims C104-C106, C135 are supported by complementation test data (Figure 3a,b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1). The viability of all non-disrupting alleles with null alleles is critical for demonstrating conditionality and is well-documented across all seven genes tested. The lack of dominant negative effects is stated but not shown in detail ('data not shown' for C106), which is a minor limitation but the positive viability data strongly supports the conclusion.

result: The VGlutFlpStop D allele resulted in significantly reduced viability when combined with a null allele but was not completely lethal, suggesting it is a hypomorphic allele. The FlpStop insertion lies between exons 3 and 4, consistent with previous work showing that deletion of exons 1-3 creates a viable hypomorphic allele.
evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by viability data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) and citation to previous work (Daniels et al., 2006). The reduced but not absent viability clearly indicates hypomorphic rather than null status. The consistency with previous deletion analysis (C112) provides independent validation of the insertion position effect. This represents a limitation of the approach for this particular gene but is honestly reported.

result: The FlpStop insert into ChAT was viable in combination with established null alleles, showing no evidence of gene disruption.
evaluation: Claim C113 is supported by complementation test data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Table 1). This represents a failure of the FlpStop approach for this particular gene (1/8 genes tested). The authors appropriately report this negative result and speculate (C84) that the complex locus structure of ChAT (with VAChT nested in the first intron) may explain the failure.

result: For X-chromosome genes para and cac, FlpStop disrupting alleles were hemizygous and homozygous lethal while non-disrupting alleles were viable. Temperature-sensitive complementation tests showed that paraFlpStop ND/parats1 flies did not become paralyzed at restrictive temperatures (33°C, 35°C), while paraFlpStop D/parats1 flies exhibited fully penetrant paralysis at both temperatures, more severe than parats1 homozygotes, indicating complete or nearly complete disruption of para function.
evaluation: Claims C114-C123 are supported by lethality observations and paralysis assay data (Figure 3c). The temperature-sensitive complementation approach is appropriate for X-chromosome genes where standard complementation tests are not feasible. The more severe phenotype of paraFlpStop D/parats1 compared to parats1/parats1 provides strong evidence for null or near-null status. Sample sizes are adequate (n=14-40 flies per condition).

result: For cac, the non-disrupting allele displayed little paralysis when complemented against cacTS2 at restrictive temperatures, while the disrupting allele (cacFlpStop D lock) displayed highly penetrant paralysis more severe than cacTS2 homozygotes, indicating severe impairment of gene function.
evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are supported by paralysis assay data (Figure 3d) with adequate sample sizes (n=50 flies per genotype and temperature). The use of the germline-inverted 'D lock' allele (C100-C101, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) is appropriate since only the non-disrupting allele was isolated by transgenesis. The more severe phenotype than homozygous temperature-sensitive mutants supports severe or complete disruption.

result: qRT-PCR analysis using primers spanning the FlpStop insertion showed that disrupting alleles reduced transcript levels by approximately 50% in heterozygotes for cac, Gad1, para, and Rdl, consistent with null allele behavior. For Shal (homozygous viable), ShalFlpStop D/ShalFlpStop D flies showed ~50% transcript reduction relative to ShalFlpStop ND/ShalFlpStop ND flies, consistent with hypomorphic function.
evaluation: Claims C127-C134 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 3e-i, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c). The primer design (C128) appropriately captures effects of both transcriptional termination and splice acceptor hijacking. The ~50% reduction in heterozygotes (C134) is the expected result for a null allele and is statistically significant (p<0.05 for all four genes tested). The Shal data (C131-C132) appropriately uses homozygotes since the gene is viable, and the 50% reduction supports hypomorphic status.

result: The FlpStop tdTomato reporter positively labels cells that have undergone cassette inversion and express Gal4. When Flp was expressed in flies carrying cacFlpStop ND, tdTomato labeled 90%, 93%, and 70% of GCaMP6f-expressing cells in Mi1, Tm1, and T4 neurons respectively. FlpStop cassettes in ap, cac, ChAT, para, Rdl, and Shal inverted efficiently (76-96% of GFP-positive cells were tdTomato-positive).
evaluation: Claims C138-C142 are supported by immunostaining and cell counting data (Figures 4-5). The quantification of inversion efficiency across multiple genes and driver lines demonstrates broad applicability. The high efficiency (70-96%) is impressive and supports the utility of the approach. The rare occurrence of tdTomato+/GCaMP6f- cells (<0.01%, C141) indicates high specificity. Sample sizes are adequate (494-1025 cells scored per condition).

result: Gad1 and VGlut FlpStop alleles showed no tdTomato expression in Mi1 neurons (a cholinergic neuron type) but did express tdTomato in other neurons when using a pan-neuronal driver. The expression patterns were distinct between the two genes but consistent across brains of the same genotype. This may reflect locus-specific silencing when genes are not expressed in a particular neuron type.
evaluation: Claims C143-C146 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The lack of tdTomato in Mi1 for Gad1 and VGlut (C143) contrasts with efficient inversion for other genes in the same cell type, indicating a locus-specific effect rather than a general problem with the Mi1 driver. The observation of tdTomato in other neurons (C144) demonstrates that the cassettes can invert and express the reporter. The speculation about locus silencing (C146) is reasonable given that Mi1 is cholinergic and would not normally express GABAergic (Gad1) or glutamatergic (VGlut) genes. The citation to Markstein et al., 2008 (C147) supports position-dependent UAS expression.

result: FlpStop cassette inversion is efficient across genes and can be achieved with multiple different Gal4 driver lines, demonstrating compatibility with existing tools for targeting specific neuronal populations.
evaluation: Claim C148 is a summary inference supported by the collective data from Figures 4-5 showing efficient inversion (70-96%) across six genes (ap, cac, ChAT, para, Rdl, Shal) using four different Gal4 drivers (Mi1, Tm1, T4, nSyb). This demonstrates both gene-independence and driver-independence of the approach, which is critical for broad applicability.

result: Cell type-specific removal of Cac in Tm3 visual interneurons selectively altered visually evoked calcium signals across subcellular compartments. Loss of Cac reduced responses in the cell body and arbors in layers Lo1 and Lo4, had no effect in layers M1, M8, and M10, and dramatically increased responses in the layer M5 dendritic arbor. This demonstrates that Cac is a critical regulator of Tm3 calcium responses with differential effects across cellular compartments.
evaluation: Claims C9, C48-C50, C173-C175, C179-C182, C223 are strongly supported by two-photon calcium imaging data (Figure 7) with appropriate controls (no-Flp and heterozygous controls) and statistical analysis (Student's t-test with Bonferroni correction). The compartment-specific effects are striking and unexpected: reduced responses in cell body, Lo1, Lo4 (p<0.01 or p<0.001); no change in M1, M8, M10; and increased responses in M5 (p<0.001). Sample sizes are adequate (38-81 cells per condition across 3-9 flies). The morphology controls (Figure 6f-k, C168-C169) rule out structural changes as an explanation. The 91% inversion efficiency (C170) and restriction of analysis to tdTomato+ cells (C171) ensure that analyzed cells are mutant.

result: To avoid developmental lethality from Tm3 driver expression in other cells during larval stages, a tub-Gal80ts transgene was used to restrict Gal4 activity to late pupal and adult stages. Experimental males and heterozygous controls expressed tdTomato in nearly all Tm3 cells by 1 day post-eclosion, while no-Flp controls showed no tdTomato. Experiments were performed in 10-12 day old adults to allow time for protein turnover.
evaluation: Claims C161-C166 are supported by experimental design description and imaging data (Figure 6b-e). The use of Gal80ts to overcome developmental lethality (C161-C163) is a standard and appropriate approach (McGuire et al., 2003). The tdTomato expression data (C164) demonstrates successful inversion. The 10-12 day waiting period (C166) is justified by estimated ion channel half-lives (Passafaro et al., 1992) and is a conservative approach to ensure complete protein turnover.

result: Despite loss of cac function substantially reducing axon branching and synaptic bouton number in larval motor neurons (prior work), confocal imaging revealed no structural changes in Tm3 morphology following FlpStop-induced loss of Cac, indicating that observed calcium signal changes are not due to gross anatomical disruptions.
evaluation: Claims C167-C169 are supported by confocal imaging data (Figure 6f-k) and citation to Rieckhof et al., 2003. The lack of morphological changes in Tm3 contrasts with motor neuron phenotypes, which is an important control demonstrating that the calcium imaging phenotypes reflect functional rather than structural changes. The imaging appears qualitative rather than quantitative, which is a minor limitation, but the lack of obvious structural differences is clear.

result: The authors speculate that the increased calcium response in layer M5 upon Cac removal may result from replacement with another calcium channel type with different properties (lower activation threshold or slower inactivation), or may reflect differential effects of compensation across subcellular compartments. Wild-type M5 calcium responses are smaller than expected from voltage signals.
evaluation: Claims C176-C178, C235-C237 are speculative explanations (explicitly labeled as speculation) for the unexpected increase in M5 calcium signals. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citation to prior work showing small M5 calcium responses relative to voltage (Yang et al., 2016, C177), these are hypotheses rather than tested conclusions. The authors appropriately acknowledge alternative explanations including compensation (C236-C237). Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish between local replacement and global compensation mechanisms.

result: The FlpStop construct uses MiMIC insertions (targeting 2854 coding introns in 1862 genes) that can be exchanged via ϕC31 integrase. The construct disrupts gene expression through transcriptional terminators (SV40, Tubα1) and a splice acceptor with stop codons in all three reading frames. These disruptive elements are flanked by FRT sites forming a FLEx-switch that enables Flp-mediated inversion and stable locking in the opposite orientation.
evaluation: Claims C51-C59 describe the design and mechanism of FlpStop, supported by Figure 1 and citations to previous work (Venken et al., 2011a; Nagarkar-Jaiswal et al., 2015b for MiMIC; Stockinger et al., 2005; Hodges and Bernstein, 1992 for disruptive elements; Schnütgen et al., 2003 for FLEx-switch). The design is clearly illustrated in Figure 1 and the mechanism is validated by the functional data throughout the paper. Similar constructs have been used successfully in flies (Lukacsovich et al., 2001; Schuldiner et al., 2008, C55) and zebrafish (Ni et al., 2012, C60).

result: FlpStop can be generalized to many genes. MiMIC insertions currently access ~24% of neuronal genes. For genes lacking suitable MiMIC sites, a CRISPR-HDR plasmid was created containing the FlpStop cassette with multiple cloning sites for homology arms and a Cre-excisable 3xP3-dsRed reporter. This enables targeting to essentially any gene with a coding intron, with more flexibility than MiMIC-based insertion for targeting specific introns.
evaluation: Claims C183-C191 are supported by the calculation of MiMIC coverage (C184, described in Materials and methods), the creation of the CRISPR-HDR plasmid (C186-C188, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and citations to CRISPR-HDR methodology (Cong et al., 2013; Gratz et al., 2014; Mali et al., 2013). The plasmid design is clearly shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The inference that this enables targeting of essentially any gene with a coding intron (C189) is reasonable. The plasmid is available from Addgene, facilitating community use.

result: The FlpStop cassette can be integrated in either orientation, enabling both conditional disruption (ND to D lock) and conditional rescue (D to ND lock). Both inverted alleles express tdTomato under Gal4 control. The disruption approach is demonstrated for essential genes, while the rescue approach is demonstrated for apterous, offering advantages over cDNA rescue by maintaining native regulatory contexts.
evaluation: Claims C192-C196 are supported by the experimental demonstrations throughout the paper. Disruption is shown for essential genes (cac, Gad1, para, Rdl) and rescue is shown for apterous (Figure 2e). The advantage of native regulatory context (C196) is a reasonable inference, though direct comparison to cDNA rescue was not performed. The bidirectional capability is a key strength of the approach.

result: FlpStop provides both spatial and temporal control through Flp expression. Heat-shock promoter control restricts inversion to brief time windows (hours to days), as demonstrated with apterous. Gal4-driven Flp expression with Gal80ts provides additional temporal specificity, as demonstrated with Tm3. Combining FlpStop with temperature-sensitive alleles enables control on the scale of seconds to minutes, as demonstrated with para and cac.
evaluation: Claims C198-C203 are supported by experimental demonstrations: heat-shock temporal control (Figure 2, C199), Gal4/Gal80ts control (Figures 6-7, C200), and temperature-sensitive allele combinations (Figure 3c,d, C202-C203). The range of temporal control from seconds to days is well-documented. The combination of spatial (cell-type specific drivers) and temporal (inducible Flp) control is a major strength of the approach.

result: FlpStop complements existing techniques for cell type-specific gene manipulation. Validated disrupting alleles are nulls with wild-type non-disrupting alleles, reducing variability compared to RNAi/deGradFP where knockdown extent varies with Gal4 strength. FlpStop's binary nature produces constant disruption in mutant cells with variable proportions. Unlike RNAi, deGradFP, and CRISPR/Cas9, FlpStop positively labels affected cells and enables rescue. Unlike MARCM, FlpStop works in post-mitotic cells. Like MARCM, FlpStop requires a null allele, though this can be avoided for X-chromosome genes using hemizygous males.
evaluation: Claims C207-C218 provide a fair comparison of FlpStop to existing methods, supported by the experimental data and established knowledge about other techniques. The advantages (null alleles, positive labeling, rescue capability, post-mitotic function) are demonstrated in the paper. The disadvantages (requires null allele, more genetic elements than RNAi) are honestly acknowledged. The comparison is balanced and helps readers understand when to use each approach. The statement that RNAi may be better for screens while FlpStop is better for targeted interrogations (C212-C213) is reasonable speculation.

result: Current cell type-specific gene disruption techniques in Drosophila (RNAi, deGradFP, recombinase-mediated deletion, CRISPR/Cas9, MARCM) have limitations including incomplete gene knockdown, dependence on Gal4 expression levels, off-target effects, lack of cell-by-cell indicators of disruption, or incompatibility with post-mitotic cells.
evaluation: Claims C1, C25-C40 describe limitations of existing methods, supported by citations to relevant literature (Dietzl et al., 2007; Caussinus et al., 2012; Hakeda-Suzuki et al., 2011; Xue et al., 2014; Lee and Luo, 1999; Ma et al., 2006). These are established facts in the field and provide appropriate context for the development of FlpStop. The characterization of limitations is accurate and fair.

result: Background claims about Drosophila as a model system, gene functions, and prior knowledge about voltage-gated channels and neurotransmission are established facts supported by appropriate citations.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C10-C24 are background knowledge claims appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the statements are consistent with established knowledge in the field.

result: Apterous is a regulator of wing development with an extensively characterized developmental role. Its disruption produces an easily quantifiable wing phenotype. Apterous is essential for wing imaginal disc development during larval stages.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65, C77 are established knowledge about apterous supported by citations (Cohen et al., 1992). This background information justifies the choice of apterous for proof-of-principle experiments and is accurate.

result: Background information about the genes targeted by FlpStop: para (voltage-gated Na+ channel), cac (voltage-gated Ca2+ channel), Shal (voltage-gated K+ channel), Gad1 (GABA synthesis enzyme), Rdl (GABAA receptor), VGlut (glutamate transporter), ChAT (acetylcholine synthesis enzyme). These genes are essential to nervous system function with null alleles being homozygous lethal.
evaluation: Claims C91-C97, C102-C103 are established knowledge about gene functions supported by appropriate citations (Suzuki et al., 1971; Loughney et al., 1989; Kawasaki et al., 2000; Butler et al., 1990; Jackson et al., 1990; Ffrench-Constant et al., 1991; Daniels et al., 2004; Greenspan, 1980). This background justifies the gene choices and is accurate.

result: Background information about Tm3: a third-order visual interneuron with branched arborizations in medulla layers M1, M5, M8, M10 and lobula layers Lo1, Lo4. M1 and M5 arbors are primarily dendritic receiving input from L1 (which receives input from R1-6 photoreceptors). M8, M10, Lo1, Lo4 arbors are primarily presynaptic. Tm3 responds to light increases with transient depolarization and calcium increases that are compartmentalized across arbors.
evaluation: Claims C149-C158 are established knowledge about Tm3 supported by appropriate citations (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Hasegawa et al., 2011; Takemura et al., 2013; Meinertzhagen et al., 1991; Behnia et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016; Ammer et al., 2015). This background provides essential context for interpreting the cac manipulation results and is accurate.

result: In motor neurons, Cac is the voltage-gated calcium channel required presynaptically for evoked neurotransmitter release. Recent studies in olfactory projection neurons suggest Cac may have a more complex role in the central nervous system.
evaluation: Claims C224-C225 are established knowledge supported by citations (Kawasaki et al., 2000, 2002; Kawasaki and Zou, 2004; Gu et al., 2009). This background provides important context for the unexpected compartment-specific effects observed in Tm3.

result: The authors hypothesized that voltage-gated calcium channels contribute to Tm3's light-evoked calcium signals and that differential distribution or regulation of specific calcium channel types underlies compartmentalization.
evaluation: Claims C159-C160 are explicitly stated as hypotheses that motivated the experiments. These are reasonable hypotheses based on prior knowledge but are not results per se. The experiments test these hypotheses and find partial support (Cac does contribute to some compartments) but also unexpected results (increased signals in M5, no effect in M1/M8/M10).

result: Speculative claims about future applications and interpretations: FlpStop will be useful for developmental studies and sensory transduction genes; combining with temperature-sensitive alleles could enable precise spatiotemporal control; RNAi may be better for screens while FlpStop is better for targeted interrogations; molecular differences in Cac requirement may be computationally significant; Cac may contribute to transcription/enzyme regulation in cell bodies; FlpStop will provide novel insights into nervous system function.
evaluation: Claims C197, C206, C212-C213, C229, C232, C241 are speculative statements about future applications or interpretations. These are reasonable speculations based on the demonstrated capabilities of FlpStop but are not tested conclusions. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than established facts.
